This vignette shows the main functions of **ls.dynam** on simulated data. The
model and the methods are described in Caimo and Gollini (2026), *Latent space
dynamic network actor models with position-rate link*.

## Model specification

In a dynamic network actor model (DyNAM) each event is the outcome of two
decisions: when an actor becomes active, and whom it selects. Actor $i$
becomes active with intensity
$$\lambda_i(t) = \exp\{\xi^\top s(i;t) + a_i\},$$
and selects receiver $j \neq i$ with probability proportional to
$\exp\{\zeta^\top s(i,j;t) + u_i^\top v_j\}$, where $u_i$ and $v_j$ are
latent sender and receiver positions. The choice model identifies the
positions only up to transformations, but it identifies the *latent
popularity* $\pi_i$, how much the average sender favours $i$ as a receiver,
and the *excess self-affinity* $\rho_i$, the preference of $i$ for actors
like itself beyond its popularity (`position_summaries()`). The
position-rate link relates them to the activity effects:
$$a_i \sim N\{\mu_a + g_\pi(\pi_i) + g_\rho(\rho_i), \sigma_a^2\},$$
with natural cubic splines $g_\pi$ and $g_\rho$. Inference is modular: the
positions are estimated from the choice of receivers alone, and the link is
estimated given them.

## Simulated data

We simulate $M = 3{,}000$ events among $n = 40$ actors, with $D = 1$ latent dimension and
activity associated with latent popularity only.

```{r simulate, cache = TRUE}
library(ls.dynam)

n <- 40; D <- 1

f <- function(x) 1.5 * (plogis(3 * x) - 0.5) # a smooth curve

tr <- make_truth(n = n, 
                 D = D, 
                 link_fun = list(pop = f, rho = NULL),
                 link_var = c("pop", "rho"), 
                 mean_u = 1, sigma_a = 0.5,
                 xi = c(rate_indeg = 0.1), 
                 zeta = c(choice_recip = 0.5), 
                 seed = 1)

ev <- simulate_lsdynam(tr$theta, 
                       n = n, 
                       M = 3000, 
                       seed = 2)
head(ev, 3)
```

The data frame of events has columns `sender`, `receiver` (labels
$1, \dots, n$) and `time`. For real data, `read_konect_events()`,
`prepare_events()`, `select_time_window()` and `filter_active_both()` produce
it (see the last section).

## Estimation

`lsdynam_fit()` fits both stages. By default the statistics are the
in-degree in the rate sub-process and reciprocity in the choice sub-process,
and the link is the additive link in latent popularity and excess
self-affinity. Here we use the Laplace approximation (`inference = "map"`),
which takes seconds; the analysis in the paper uses posterior simulation
(see below).

```{r fit, cache = TRUE}
fit <- lsdynam_fit(ev, 
                   n = n, 
                   D = D, 
                   inference = "map", 
                   n_starts = 3, 
                   verbose = FALSE)

summary(fit)
```

The contrasts compare the level of each component at the 90% and 10%
quantiles of its summary, and the log Bayes factors test the whole link and
each component given the other. `plot()` shows the components of the link;
the rug marks the actors' values.

```{r link-plot, cache = TRUE}
plot(fit)
```

The truth is a step in popularity and no effect of excess self-affinity. The
contrasts and Bayes factors can also be obtained directly:

```{r link-summaries, cache = TRUE}
ct <- link_contrast(fit, "pop")

round(c(estimate = ct$mean, 
        lower = ct$ci[1], 
        upper = ct$ci[2]), 2)

# excess self-affinity given popularity
link_evidence(fit, components = "rho")$log_bf10_laplace   
```

Links in other summaries can be compared on the same positions by their log
marginal likelihoods; the difference between `"pop + rho"` and `"pop"` is
the log Bayes factor for excess self-affinity given popularity.

```{r comparison, cache = TRUE}
cmp <- link_comparison_table(fit, 
                             list("pop + rho" = c("pop", "rho"), 
                                  pop = "pop",
                                  rho = "rho", r = "r"))

cmp$table[, c("link", "K", "sigma_a", "log_ml_vs_M1", "R2")]
```

With one dimension the positions can be displayed. Filled points have
positive self-affinity.

```{r positions, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9, out.width = "100%", cache = TRUE}
plot_positions(fit, ellipses = FALSE)
```

## Prediction

The models are compared on held-out events: $\mathcal{M}_0$ has no latent
positions, $\mathcal{M}_1$ has positions but no link, and $\mathcal{M}_2$ has
both. The choice score compares $\mathcal{M}_1$ with $\mathcal{M}_0$, the
rate score $\mathcal{M}_2$ with $\mathcal{M}_1$.

```{r prediction, cache = TRUE}
m_tr <- 2400
train <- ev[seq_len(m_tr), ]

m0 <- lsdynam_fit(train, 
                  n = n, 
                  D = 0, 
                  inference = "map", 
                  verbose = FALSE)

m2 <- lsdynam_fit(train, 
                  n = n, 
                  D = 1, 
                  inference = "map", 
                  verbose = FALSE)

m1 <- lsdynam_fit(train, 
                  n = n, 
                  D = 1, 
                  link = "none", 
                  inference = "map",
                  choice = m2$choice, 
                  verbose = FALSE)

sc <- lapply(list(M0 = m0, 
                  M1 = m1, 
                  M2 = m2), 
             predictive_scores,
             events_full = ev, 
             n = n, 
             m_train = m_tr, 
             n_draws = 100)

rbind("M1 - M0" = score_difference(sc$M1, sc$M0)[2, 2:4],
      "M2 - M1" = score_difference(sc$M2, sc$M1)[1, 2:4])
```

The latent positions improve the prediction of the receivers considerably.
The link improves the rate score only slightly, because the rate of an actor
who has sent many events is determined by its own record: it describes how
activity varies with position rather than improving the forecast of when
actors send.

## Posterior simulation

The analysis of the paper simulates both modules with a Metropolis-adjusted
Langevin algorithm (MALA), from many starting configurations of the choice module,
and adds the cut posterior.

```{r mcmc, eval = TRUE, cache = TRUE}
fit <- lsdynam_fit(ev, 
                   n = n, 
                   D = D, 
                   n_iter = 12000, 
                   burn_in = 2000, 
                   thin = 5,
                   n_starts = 10, 
                   n_cut = 300)

mcmc_diagnostics(fit)                   

plot_traces(fit)

plot(fit) # plug-in (shaded) and cut (dashed) posteriors

link_evidence(fit, 
              components = "rho", 
              sigma_kappa_grid = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2))

# reference distributions: no association, and popularity only
cal0 <- null_link_calibration(fit, n_rep = 10)
cal1 <- null_link_calibration(fit, n_rep = 10, keep = "pop")
```

## Real data

The Radoslaw e-mail data are available from the KONECT collection
(<https://konect.cc/networks/radoslaw_email>). The analysis of the paper
used the second fifth of the observation period and the actors who both
send and receive in it.

```{r real, eval = FALSE}
ev <- read_konect_events("out.radoslaw_email_email")

ev <- prepare_events(ev) 

ev <- select_time_window(ev, 
                         start_frac = 0.2, 
                         end_frac = 0.4)

fa <- filter_active_both(ev)

fit <- lsdynam_fit(fa$events_df, 
                   n = fa$n, 
                   D = 2, 
                   n_iter = 12000, 
                   burn_in = 2000,
                   thin = 5, 
                   n_starts = 30, 
                   n_cut = 300)
```
